Entries.Text: Collision Editor
Collision Editor
This tool is only supported for Dark Souls III, Sekiro, Elden Ring, Nightreign, Armored Core VI and The Duskbloods (Network Test).

Reshape, create and wall map collision. Edit moves the vertices of the displayed collision; Create adds a new collision to the active map; Fall Protection builds the walls that stop falls off a collision's edges; Cleanup removes collision files no part uses.
How this works
The steps of this tab. Open the first time the tab is shown; the eye shows or hides them.

1. Choose the Layer to edit (show it if it is hidden), then Start Collision Edit.
2. Move the mouse over the collision: the cursor marks the vertex that moves, and the Cursor section says how many move with it. Raise and lower it with the keys, or hold the drag key to slide it at its height.
3. A Radius moves the vertices around it too; with Link High and Low on, the other layer follows.
4. Commit (above the tabs) rebuilds the edited files and writes them into the project; Discard puts the vertices back.

1. Check the Map: the collision is made for the active map.
2. Choose a Shape: a basic shape (made at the placement orb), the FLVERs of the selected map pieces and assets, or User-Defined points placed in the viewport. Set its Facing, Material and size.
3. Keep the suggested Model ID, or type one. An ID the map already uses overwrites that collision, once confirmed.
4. Create writes the new h and l files into the project and adds a part placing them (saved with the map). The buttons under the result select it or go on to its fall protection.

1. Select one collision part, or pick it from the list. Fall Protection for It (Create) and Regenerate Walls (after a commit) bring you here with it selected.
2. Choose the Source Layer whose outer edges the walls follow, and the Direction. Drop Edges Only leaves out seams and the edges of walls and ceilings.
3. Check the walls in the viewport and the counts, then Generate. They go in the model's f file, written into the project, as one undo.
Only Elden Ring, Nightreign and The Duskbloods (Network Test) have walls this tab can build.
Glossary
The collision terms the tool uses.
Layers (high, low, fall protection)

A collision model has up to three layers, each a file of its own: high (h) and low (l) are the same ground at two levels of detail, h the more detailed; fall protection (f) is a set of thin walls along edges. Each layer is drawn and edited separately.
Collision files
Named for the layer, map and model: h10_00_00_00_002400.hkx.dcx is the high collision of model h002400 in m10_00_00_00, and l... and f... are its other layers.
Binder
The archive holding every file of one layer of a map (its h, l or f files). Committing, creating or generating writes the whole binder into the project.
Body
A shape inside a collision file. An h or l file holds one body, a compressed mesh of triangles; an f file holds one body per run of wall.
Model and collision part

A model is a collision's mesh, known by h and six digits (h002400). A collision part is the map entry that places a model; several parts can place one model, and all of them show its mesh, so an edit changes every one.
Linked layers
High and low don't share vertices, so with Link High and Low on, an edit of one moves the other's vertices near the edited one: fully within the link distance, fading out past it with the radius.
Radius
How far around the cursor's vertex an edit reaches. Vertices nearer it move more; those past the radius don't move. 0 moves the vertex alone.
Facing
Which side of a triangle is solid. Ground faces up. If a new collision can be fallen or walked through in game, try the other facing.
Collision material
The material each triangle carries, picked by name. A FLVER mesh whose material is named hkm_Name_Property keeps that material.
Placement orb
The marker in front of the camera where new objects are placed (viewport Settings > Placement Orb). Basic shapes are created there, and the first Gizmo point is spawned there.
Fall protection

Thin vertical walls that stop falls off the edges of collision. The game doesn't protect every drop, and its walls follow the walkable edge rather than the collision's, so generated walls are a starting point.
Drop edges
Outer edges of ground that can be stood on, with nothing, or ground well below, just past them. Drop Edges Only gives walls to these alone, leaving out open seams between pieces of floor.
Collision filter
A value on each fall protection body. The game's walls use 0 or 1; copy the value of the map's other walls.
Commit and saving

Moved vertices are a preview until committed. Commit, Create and Generate write their files into the project at once. Their undo and redo show in the viewport straight away and reach the files when the map is saved; a created part is saved with the map.
Viewport
Whether collision is drawn, what the viewport's clicks, keys and gizmo do, and edits that haven't been committed. Shown on every tab.
Show Collision

The viewport's collision filter, as in the Filters menu. Collision must be shown to be edited, and for the previews to be seen. Which layers (high, low, fall protection) are drawn is set separately; the Edit tab offers to show the layer it edits.

Actions
Start or stop editing. Commit and Discard are above the tabs, shown while there are edits.
Start Collision Edit

Shows the cursor on the collision under the mouse, so its vertices can be moved with the keys below. Turns off the Navigation tool's vertex editing, which uses the same keys. Editing stops when this tab is left or the Collision Editor is closed; edits that haven't been committed are kept, and Commit and Discard appear above the tabs.
Stop Collision Edit
Hides the cursor. Edits that haven't been committed are kept, and can be committed or discarded later.
Commit Changes

Rebuilds the edited collision from the moved vertices and writes the collision binders it is in into the project straight away. Can be undone: the undo shows in the viewport at once, and reaches the project's files when the map is saved.
Discard Changes
Puts every moved vertex back where it was.
Layer
The collision layer the cursor edits. Only this layer is hit, as the layers lie on top of each other.
High and low collision are the same ground at two levels of detail. Fall protection is a barrier of its own.
{0} collision isn't displayed, so the cursor can't be placed on it.
Display {0} Collision
Displays this collision layer for every collision part.
Linked Layers
Whether the other layer of a part follows the edits, so high and low collision stay on the same ground.
Link High and Low

Moves the vertices of the other layer near the edited vertex by the same amount, and commits both files. The layers don't share vertices, and don't always cover the same ground, so only vertices within the link distance follow. Works whether or not the other layer is displayed.
{0} collision isn't linked to another layer.
{0} collision follows edits to {1} collision.
Link Distance
How close the other layer's vertices must be to the edited vertex to follow it fully. Past it, the radius fades them out.
The distance in world units. Most low vertices lie within 0.5 of the high collision; larger distances may pull in nearby surfaces that aren't the same ground.
Linked: {0}, {1} of its vertices follow.
Linked: {0}, but none of its vertices are within the link distance, so it doesn't follow here.
An edit here moves {0} vertices (radius {1}).
Cursor Display
The size and opacity of the cursor sphere. Rarely changed, so hidden by default.
Linked: none (this part has no other layer that can be edited)
Step
How far each press of the raise or lower key moves the vertex.
The distance in world units, up or down.
Radius
Moves the vertices around the target as well, less the further they are from it.
The distance in world units. 0 moves the target vertex alone.
Cursor Size
The size of the cursor sphere. The vertex marker is a little smaller.
The radius in world units.
Cursor Opacity
How solid the fill inside the cursor's wireframe is. Lower lets the collision under a large cursor show through.
0% leaves the wireframe alone; 100% fills the cursor solid.
Controls
The keys work while the mouse is over the viewport and no mouse button is held, as the mouse buttons fly the camera with the same keys. They can be changed in the keybind settings.
{0}: raise the vertex.
{0}: lower the vertex.
Hold {0}: drag the vertex across the ground at its height.

Fall Protection
Generate the fall protection collision of the selected collision part: flat vertical walls along the outer edges of its high or low collision, written into its fall protection (f) file.
Fall protection can only be generated for Elden Ring, Nightreign and The Duskbloods (Network Test).
Collision Part
The collision part the walls are made for. They go in the f file of its model, which every part placing the model uses.
Select a single collision part to generate its fall protection.
{0} (model {1}, map {2})

Source Layer
The collision whose outer edges the walls follow.
High or low collision of the part's model. The two usually cover the same ground.
The part's model has no {0} to follow.

Direction
Which outer edges get walls, by the way they face in the world.

All edges, or only those facing one way: north is +Z and east is +X, as the open world's map numbers go up. An edge faces away from the collision it is the edge of, and counts for the direction it is nearest.
All
North (+Z)
East (+X)
South (-Z)
West (-X)
Drop Edges
Whether only the outer edges that can be fallen off get walls.
Drop Edges Only

On, an outer edge gets a wall only if it is the edge of ground that can be stood on (facing up, slopes up to about 60 degrees) and, just past it, the ground of this part and the loaded collision parts around it is more than the minimum drop lower, or missing. Open seams between pieces of floor, and the edges of walls and ceilings, then get no walls. Off, every outer edge gets one.
How far below an edge the ground past it must be for the edge to be a drop, in world units. Ground up to 0.5 above the edge counts as ground too.
{0} of them are drops, with the collision of {1} other parts as ground.
No outer edge facing that way is a drop, so there is nothing to generate.
Wall Height
How far the walls reach above the edges they stand on.
In world units. Every wall in the game's fall protection is 1.8 high.
Collision Filter
The collision filter info of the wall bodies.
The game's walls use 0 or 1; Elden Ring's legacy dungeons only use 1. Copy the value of the map's other walls.
Existing Walls
What happens to the walls the f file already has.
{0} has {1} wall bodies.
Keep Existing Walls
On, the new walls are added to the file's walls, e.g. to add one direction at a time. Off, they replace them.
Preview
The walls that will be generated, drawn in the viewport in the fall protection colour while this tab is open.
Show in Viewport
Draws the walls in the viewport, placed with the part. Collision must be shown (Show Collision above the tabs).
{0} outer edges, {1} facing the direction: {2} walls in {3} bodies.
No outer edge faces that way, so there is nothing to generate.

Line
A vertical wall along the points, from each point up by the height.
Plane
The outline the points make, filled. Each corner is at its point's own height, so points placed on flat ground make a flat plane.
Box

The outline the points make, extruded into a closed solid: the floor at the lowest point, the roof the height above the highest. Two points make a rectangle along the world axes, with them as opposite corners.
How the placed points become the collision's triangles.
Height
How far the wall reaches above each point.
How far the roof is above the highest point.
Closed Loop
Also join the last point back to the first, so the wall goes all the way round. Needs 3 points.
Flip Facing
Turn the wall to face the other side. Without it, the wall faces left of the direction the points were placed in, seen from above. If the wall can be walked through in game, try the other side.
Up for faces pointing out of the box (the floor down, the roof up, the walls out). If the box can be walked into in game, try the other facing.
Points
The points the shape is made from, placed by raycast (clicking on what the viewport draws) or spawned and moved with the gizmo. Click a placed point's sphere to move it with the gizmo.
Raycast
Place each point by clicking in the viewport: it lands where the click meets the map.
Gizmo
Spawn points with Add Point and move each with the gizmo. Points can be placed anywhere, including in the air or inside the map.
How points are placed. Placed points can be moved with the gizmo in either mode, by clicking their spheres.

Click in the viewport to add a point after the last one.

Collision Material
The collision material of the triangles. A FLVER mesh whose material is named hkm_Name_Property keeps that material.
Parameters
The size of the shape, in world units.
Width
The size of the square along X.
Length
The size of the square along Z.
Size
The length of the triangle's sides.
Radius
The distance from the centre to the edge.
Segments
How many triangles make up the curve. More is smoother.

Meshes
Which meshes of each FLVER go into the collision.
All
Use every mesh of every FLVER.
None
Use no meshes, to pick a few.
Simplify
A pass over the combined FLVER mesh that reduces its detail while keeping its general shape, so the collision has far fewer triangles than the render mesh.
The mesh is simplified.
Simplify Mesh

Collapse the mesh's edges, cheapest first, until the target is reached or every further collapse would move the surface by more than the max error. Flat areas reduce the most; slopes, steps and creases keep their shape.
Target
The share of the triangles to keep. Fewer may be kept when the max error stops the pass first.
Max Error
How far, in metres, the simplified surface may stray from the original. Lower keeps more detail; higher reduces further.
Keep Borders

Never move the vertices on the mesh's open edges or on the borders between collision materials, so it still meets neighbouring collision exactly and each material keeps its area. Off, they may move, but at a heavy cost.
Simplified from {0} to {1} triangles ({2}%).

The number of the new collision model: the part's model is h followed by it, and its files are named for it.
Six digits. Suggested as the first unused number after the map's highest below 900000.
The model ID must be six digits.

Cleanup

1. Find Unused lists the collision files of the active map that no part of its MSB uses. A part with model h001234 uses the h, l and f files ending _001234, whether the part is enabled or not.
2. Every listed file starts ticked; untick the ones to keep. Your choice is kept when you scan the same map again.
3. Cleanup removes the ticked files from the map's collision binders and writes the binders into the project straight away. This can't be undone.
4. The MSB as it is now in the editor is what counts: if you deleted a part and don't save the map, the game still has that part but no longer its collision. Save the map after a cleanup.
Files with uncommitted edits, files whose names don't follow the usual pattern, and the last collision file of a binder are always kept.
Remove the collision files of the active map that no part uses.
